\chapter{Tools}
\label{ch:te-tools}
\hlchaptermodality{69}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name five Telugu tools and ask politely to borrow one.}

\section[goḍḍali]{\te{గొడ్డలి} (goḍḍali) — an axe}

\label{lesson:TE-C69-axe}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{kaburu} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{గొడ్డలి}}
\textbf{\te{గొడ్డలి}} (\emph{goḍḍali}) — \textquotedblleft{}an axe\textquotedblright{}.

\te{గొడ్డలి} is an axe — an iron head on a wooden handle, for cutting a \te{చెట్టు} down or splitting firewood at the \te{గడప}.

The word is inherited and old. Its first piece turns up in other Telugu words about striking, so the name says plainly what the thing does.

Asking for one is the ordinary polite request: \te{దయచేసి}, and then the word. The person hands it over handle first, and nobody throws a \te{గొడ్డలి}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One. Heavy, and handed over rather than thrown.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{goḍḍali}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{dayacēsi}, then \emph{goḍḍali}, in that order
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{గొడ్డలి} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}an axe\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[rampaṁ]{\te{రంపం} (rampaṁ) — a saw}

\label{lesson:TE-C69-saw}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{goḍḍali} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{రంపం}}
\textbf{\te{రంపం}} (\emph{rampaṁ}) — \textquotedblleft{}a saw\textquotedblright{}.

\te{రంపం} is a saw. Where the \te{గొడ్డలి} breaks wood apart, the \te{రంపం} takes it apart along a line.

It is a borrowing, and it came in with the trade rather than ahead of it: the long two-man saw and its name reached the carpenter's shed together.

The noise is half the word. Telugu calls a rasping sound a \te{రంపం} sound, and somebody who repeats a complaint until you give way is running a \te{రంపం} over your \te{చెవి}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two. Both of them cut; only one cuts straight.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{rampaṁ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{goḍḍali}, then \emph{rampaṁ}, and say which one leaves a straight edge
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{రంపం} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a saw\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pāra]{\te{పార} (pāra) — a spade}

\label{lesson:TE-C69-spade}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{rampaṁ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{పార}}
\textbf{\te{పార}} (\emph{pāra}) — \textquotedblleft{}a spade\textquotedblright{}.

\te{పార} is a spade — a broad iron blade on a handle, for digging and for shifting \te{బురద} or \te{ఇసుక}.

It is the tool of the \te{రైతు} out of season: clearing a channel, banking up the edge of a \te{పొలం}, cutting a way for water to run.

The word is inherited and it stays narrow. It does not stretch into anything figurative at all, which by itself says how firmly it belongs to the ground.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three. The first one here you push rather than swing.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{pāra}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{pāra}, then \emph{rampaṁ}, and say which one you push
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{పార} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a spade\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sutti]{\te{సుత్తి} (sutti) — a hammer}

\label{lesson:TE-C69-hammer}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{pāra} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{సుత్తి}}
\textbf{\te{సుత్తి}} (\emph{sutti}) — \textquotedblleft{}a hammer\textquotedblright{}.

\te{సుత్తి} is a hammer: an iron head on a short handle, for driving things in and for beating things straight.

Telugu turned it into a word about people. Somebody who makes the same point until you give in is doing \te{సుత్తి}, and telling them to stop the \te{సుత్తి} is telling them to stop going on.

In a city that second sense is now the commoner one, which is worth knowing before somebody uses it about you.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four. The one whose second meaning you are likelier to hear.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{sutti}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{sutti}, then \emph{goḍḍali}, and say which one has a short handle
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{సుత్తి} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a hammer\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[karra]{\te{కర్ర} (karra) — a stick}

\label{lesson:TE-C69-stick}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{sutti} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{కర్ర}}
\textbf{\te{కర్ర}} (\emph{karra}) — \textquotedblleft{}a stick\textquotedblright{}.

\te{కర్ర} is a stick — a length of wood, cut or picked up, for everything the other four are too particular for.

It is inherited and completely ordinary: a walking stick for a \te{తాత}, a herding stick behind a \te{మేక}, the handle still waiting for a \te{గొడ్డలి} head.

It is also the right thing to ask for first. \te{దయచేసి} and a \te{కర్ర} costs nobody anything, and by the time you want the \te{సుత్తి} you already know how to ask.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five: \te{గొడ్డలి}, \te{రంపం}, \te{పార}, \te{సుత్తి}, \te{కర్ర}. Enough to ask for anything in a shed.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{karra}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order, then \emph{dayacēsi} and the one you would borrow first
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{కర్ర} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a stick\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
